clinicalPearls: A localised posterior bulge of the posterior lens capsule and cortex into the vitreous, usually unilateral, sporadic and more common than anterior lenticonus
It is an important cause of unilateral acquired or progressive cataract and amblyopia in infancy and childhood, and warrants early paediatric ophthalmology referral
Retro-illumination shows a central 'oil-droplet' or fish-tail reflex, and the posterior curvature may progress with growth, later opacifying into a posterior polar or lamellar cataract
The overlying posterior capsule is inherently thin and prone to spontaneous dehiscence, so a pre-existing or intra-operative posterior capsule defect should be anticipated
Because it is frequently unilateral and progressive, dense amblyopia is a major threat and mandates refractive correction and occlusion alongside any surgery
Most cases are isolated, but posterior lenticonus can occur in Lowe (oculocerebrorenal) syndrome and, less often, in the Alport spectrum, prompting a directed systemic review
Surgical planning should account for the weak or absent posterior capsule, with a low threshold for anterior vitrectomy and careful intraocular lens placement
Ultrasound or anterior segment imaging helps define the posterior lens contour and detect any capsular breach before intervention
reference.pathophysiology: Posterior lenticonus arises from a focal area of weakness and thinning in the posterior lens capsule, which normally lacks the epithelial support present anteriorly. The exact mechanism is debated but proposed causes include a primary developmental defect of the posterior capsule, abnormal persistence or traction of the hyaloid vascular system on the posterior pole, and relative overgrowth of lens fibres against a deficient capsule. The weakened region bulges backward under intralenticular forces, increasing local curvature and lens power; progressive stretching disrupts the adjacent cortical fibres and leads to focal opacification and eventual posterior polar cataract. Frank dehiscence of the attenuated capsule can occur spontaneously.
additionalDifferentials: Persistent fetal vasculature (persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous)
Lamellar or total congenital cataract of other cause
Retinoblastoma or other cause of leukocoria in a child
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with retro-illumination to demonstrate the posterior conical bulge and any opacity
Retinoscopy and cycloplegic refraction to detect the oil-droplet reflex and anisometropia
B-scan ultrasonography or anterior segment OCT to define posterior lens contour and integrity of the posterior capsule
Assessment for amblyopia with age-appropriate visual acuity testing and fixation preference
Systemic and metabolic evaluation for Lowe syndrome where clinically suspected
Fundus examination to exclude persistent fetal vasculature and posterior segment pathology
redFlags: Dense unilateral cataract in an infant with high risk of irreversible deprivation amblyopia
Evidence of spontaneous posterior capsule rupture with sudden lens swelling or fragments in the vitreous
Leukocoria requiring urgent exclusion of retinoblastoma
Rapid progression of lens opacity or myopic shift in the amblyogenic period
reference.prognosis: With timely surgery, intraocular lens implantation and rigorous amblyopia therapy the visual prognosis for isolated posterior lenticonus can be favourable, though outcome depends heavily on the depth of amblyopia at presentation. Cases complicated by posterior capsule rupture or dense long-standing amblyopia have a more guarded visual outlook.
pitfalls: Delaying referral and surgery so that dense amblyopia becomes irreversible
Being unprepared for a pre-existing posterior capsule defect during cataract surgery
Mistaking the oil-droplet reflex for a corneal or vitreous abnormality
Neglecting occlusion therapy after successful lens surgery
Failing to consider Lowe syndrome or other systemic associations
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course (Paediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus)
management: Refer urgently to paediatric ophthalmology given the threat of dense amblyopia from a unilateral progressive lens opacity
Perform lens extraction with intraocular lens implantation once a visually significant cataract or bulging lens develops
Anticipate a thin or dehiscent posterior capsule intra-operatively and plan for anterior vitrectomy and appropriate lens fixation
Institute vigorous amblyopia therapy with cycloplegic refractive correction and occlusion of the sound eye alongside any surgery
Monitor refraction and lens contour over time, as posterior curvature may progress with growth before opacifying
Undertake systemic and metabolic evaluation for Lowe syndrome and the Alport spectrum where suspected, with appropriate paediatric and genetic referral
